lesson.title: Network Function Virtualization: Trading Boxes for Software
lesson.summary: NFV replaces dedicated hardware appliances, firewalls, load balancers, and similar devices, with software equivalents that run as virtual machines or containers on standard servers instead of purpose built hardware.
lesson.body:
SDN and NFV are often mentioned together, and both emerged around the same period in networking's shift toward software, but they solve different problems. SDN is about separating the control plane from the data plane and centralizing forwarding decisions. Network function virtualization is about something else: taking network functions, firewalls, load balancers, intrusion detection systems, WAN optimizers, that used to require dedicated, purpose built hardware appliances, and running them instead as software on standard, general purpose servers.

For decades, adding a new network function to a site meant buying a physical box. A firewall was a specific piece of hardware, built and sold by a specific vendor, installed in a specific rack, with a fixed amount of processing capacity that could not grow or shrink without buying and installing another box. If a data center needed more load balancing capacity during a busy season, someone had to order, ship, rack, and cable another physical load balancer, a process that could take weeks and left expensive hardware sitting idle the rest of the year. NFV replaces that physical appliance with a virtual network function, a VNF, a piece of software that performs the same job, packaged as a virtual machine or container image that can run on any sufficiently capable server in a pool of shared, general purpose hardware.

Consider a telecom operator running dozens of regional sites, each of which used to need its own rack of dedicated firewall appliances, deep packet inspection boxes, and load balancers. With NFV, those functions become software instances running on shared commodity servers at each site, or even centralized further back in the network. When traffic spikes, the operator can spin up additional firewall VNF instances on existing spare server capacity in minutes rather than ordering new hardware. When the spike passes, those instances can be torn down, freeing the server capacity for something else. The function itself, filtering traffic according to firewall rules, has not changed. What changed is that it no longer needs its own dedicated box to run on.

NFV and SDN complement each other well in practice, even though they address different layers of the problem. An SDN controller can direct traffic through a chain of VNFs, routing a flow through a virtual firewall, then a virtual load balancer, in whatever order a policy requires, something that is awkward to do with fixed hardware appliances wired into specific physical positions in a network. This combination, software defined forwarding directing traffic through software defined functions, is a major part of how modern telecom and cloud infrastructure, including much of the equipment behind 5G networks, is generally described as being built today.
